section.title: The Grain Offering
section.sectionRationale: The second of the five great offerings, the grain offering is bloodless, made of fine flour, oil, and frankincense. It continues the sacrificial law collection begun in chapter one, showing that worship of God involves the fruit of ordinary labor as well as the blood of animals.
section.thesis: The grain offering, seasoned with salt and free of leaven or honey, teaches Israel to bring the best of their labor to God as a memorial offering, most holy, a portion given wholly to Him and to His priests.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the offering of raw flour and oil; the offering baked, on a griddle, or in a pan; the prohibitions of leaven and honey and the requirement of salt; and the offering of firstfruits.

units.label: Flour, oil, and frankincense
units.note: a memorial portion burned to the LORD

verses.text: “When anyone brings a {{minchah|grain offering}} to the LORD, his offering must consist of fine flour. He is to pour olive oil on it, put frankincense on it,

and bring it to Aaron's sons the priests. The priest shall take a handful of the flour and oil, together with all the frankincense, and burn this as a memorial portion on the altar, an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
The remainder of the grain offering shall belong to Aaron and his sons; it is a {{qodeshQodashim|most holy}} part of the offerings made by fire to the LORD.

units.label: Baked, on a griddle, or in a pan
units.note: three prepared forms of the same offering

verses.text: Now if you bring an offering of grain baked in an oven, it must consist of fine flour, either unleavened cakes mixed with oil or unleavened wafers coated with oil.
If your offering is a grain offering prepared on a griddle, it must be unleavened bread made of fine flour mixed with oil.
Crumble it and pour oil on it; it is a grain offering.
If your offering is a grain offering cooked in a pan, it must consist of fine flour with oil.
When you bring to the LORD the grain offering made in any of these ways, it is to be presented to the priest, and he shall take it to the altar.
The priest is to remove the memorial portion from the grain offering and burn it on the altar as an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
But the remainder of the grain offering shall belong to Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the offerings made by fire to the LORD.

units.label: No leaven, no honey, only salt

verses.text: No grain offering that you present to the LORD may be made with leaven, for you are not to burn any leaven or honey as an offering made by fire to the LORD.
You may bring them to the LORD as an offering of firstfruits, but they are not to be offered on the altar as a pleasing aroma.

And you shall season each of your grain offerings with {{melach|salt}}. You must not leave the salt of the covenant of your God out of your grain offering; you are to add salt to each of your offerings.
If you bring a grain offering of firstfruits to the LORD, you shall offer crushed heads of new grain roasted on the fire.
And you are to put oil and frankincense on it; it is a grain offering.
The priest shall then burn the memorial portion of the crushed grain and the oil, together with all its frankincense, as an offering made by fire to the LORD.

minchah.gloss: A grain offering or gift, sometimes used of a tribute given to a superior. This bloodless offering of flour, oil, and frankincense honors God with the fruit of ordinary daily labor, not only with animal sacrifice.

qodeshQodashim.gloss: Most holy, or holy of holies, the highest degree of consecration. What remains of the grain offering is set at this level, meaning only priests could eat it, and only in a holy place.

melach.gloss: The salt of the covenant. Salt preserves and does not decay, so its required presence in every grain offering pictures the permanence and faithfulness of God's covenant with His people, compare Numbers 18:19 and 2 Chronicles 13:5.

basic.context: After the burnt offering, God gives instructions for the grain offering, a bloodless gift of fine flour, oil, and frankincense. Unlike the burnt offering, most of it belonged to the priests to eat, though a memorial portion was always burned to God. It could be raw, baked, griddled, or pan cooked, but it always had to include salt and never leaven or honey.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes an actual old covenant ritual for Israel, not a pattern Christians are to reenact. Its abiding truth is that God is honored not only through costly blood sacrifice but through the ordinary produce of daily work, offered without corruption and seasoned with covenant faithfulness.
basic.originalLanguages: Minchah, grain offering, can also mean tribute or gift, showing that this offering honors God as a superior worthy of gifts from His people's labor. The remainder is qodesh qodashim, most holy, and every offering required melach berit, the salt of the covenant, a symbol of God's unbreakable faithfulness.
basic.typology: The fine, unleavened flour points toward the sinless perfection of Christ, since leaven throughout Scripture often pictures corruption or sin working through a whole batch. The salt of the covenant anticipates the permanence of the new covenant sealed in Christ's blood, a covenant that, unlike salt's endurance, will never decay.
basic.christ: Christ is the true bread from heaven, John 6:35, offered without the leaven of sin, 1 Peter 2:22. As the grain offering was crushed and burned, so Christ was crushed for our iniquities, Isaiah 53:5, His life given as a fragrant offering to God, Ephesians 5:2.
basic.god: God delights to receive not only blood sacrifice but the honest fruit of daily labor, showing that worship touches every part of ordinary life, not merely the dramatic or costly. His covenant faithfulness, pictured in salt that never decays, means His promises to His people never spoil or fail.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 5:2 calls Christ's self giving a fragrant offering to God. 1 Corinthians 5:6-8 warns that a little leaven leavens the whole batch, urging believers to keep the feast without the leaven of malice. Numbers 18:19 calls God's covenant with the priesthood a covenant of salt.
basic.oneStory: The grain offering teaches Israel that worship includes the ordinary fruit of daily labor, offered without corruption and sealed by the enduring salt of the covenant. It anticipates Christ, the unleavened bread of life, crushed and offered as a pleasing aroma so that God's covenant faithfulness to His people would never fail.

context.literary:
Leviticus 2 follows the pattern of chapter 1, a list of cases each closing in a set formula, but it changes key. There is no animal, no hand laid on a head, no slaughter and no blood. The chapter is about flour, oil, incense and salt, and it reads almost like a recipe, with the tools of an Israelite kitchen named one by one: the oven, the griddle and the pan, verses 4, 5 and 7.

The chapter falls into two main cases and two appendices. Verses 1 to 3 describe uncooked flour with oil and frankincense. Verses 4 to 10 describe the offering already baked or fried. Both units end with the same line, 'The remainder of the grain offering shall belong to Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the offerings made by fire to the LORD,' verses 3 and 10. That repeated sentence frames the heart of the chapter and makes the priests' share part of the offering's meaning, not an afterthought. Verses 11 to 13 then give general rules for every grain offering, no leaven or honey and always salt, and verses 14 to 16 add a special case, the firstfruits of new grain.

The voice also shifts. Verse 1 speaks of 'anyone' in the third person, as chapter 1 did. From verse 4 onward the law turns to 'you': 'if you bring,' 'if your offering.' The move from case law to direct address draws the hearer in, as though Moses were speaking to a household deciding what to bring.

The grain offering is placed after the burnt offering and before the peace offering, and that is how it usually functioned. Grain accompanied the daily burnt offering, Exodus 29:40-41, and Numbers 15:3-4 requires a grain offering with every burnt offering or sacrifice. Chapter 2 treats it separately so its own meaning can be heard: a gift of the field set beside the gift of the flock.
context.historical:
Israel was about to become a settled farming people in 'a land of wheat, barley, vines, fig trees, and pomegranates; a land of olive oil and honey,' Deuteronomy 8:8. The grain offering prepared them to see the harvest as God's gift and to give part of it back to Him. Flour, oil and salt were the staples of every kitchen; frankincense was not. It came from far away, and Jeremiah names 'frankincense from Sheba,' Jeremiah 6:20, the southern Arabian trade. All of it was burned, verses 2 and 16, so the one costly import in the offering went entirely to God.

The fine flour of verse 1 was more carefully milled than ordinary household meal, which gave the offering a certain value. Yet the grain offering also sat at the bottom of the scale of costs. Leviticus 5:11 allows someone who cannot afford even two birds to bring 'a tenth of an ephah of fine flour' as a sin offering, without oil or frankincense. Flour was within reach of the poorest.

The priests depended on this offering. They were given 'no inheritance in their land,' because 'I am your portion and your inheritance,' Numbers 18:20. The remainder of every grain offering fed them. It was 'most holy,' so it had to be eaten by the males of Aaron's family, without leaven, 'in a holy place,' in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting, Leviticus 6:16-18. The baked kinds went to the officiating priest, while the dry kinds were shared among all the priests, Leviticus 7:9-10.

Leaven had a sharp association for this generation. They had left Egypt with dough that had no leaven, Exodus 12:39, and the Passover required every trace of it to be removed from their houses, Exodus 12:15. The same instinct governs the altar: 'You must not offer the blood of My sacrifices with anything leavened,' Exodus 23:18. The firstfruits of verse 14, roasted heads of new grain, were a familiar food of harvest time, the 'roasted grain' Boaz offered Ruth, Ruth 2:14.
context.canonical:
The word for this offering reaches back to the first worship outside Eden. Cain and Abel each brought an 'offering,' the same word minchah, Genesis 4:3-5. Only later does Leviticus fix the word to grain. The distinction between the grain offering and the animal offerings, and the requirement of salt, then runs through Israel's worship. Ezekiel's vision of a restored temple still has the priests 'sprinkle salt' on the offerings, Ezekiel 43:24. Numbers 18:19 calls the priests' share of the holy offerings 'a permanent covenant of salt,' and 2 Chronicles 13:5 uses the same phrase for God's covenant with David's house.

The grain offering becomes a picture of prayer and a measure of spiritual health. 'May my prayer be set before You like incense, my uplifted hands like the evening offering,' Psalm 141:2, uses minchah for the evening sacrifice. Elijah prayed on Carmel 'at the time of the evening sacrifice,' 1 Kings 18:36. When Joel mourns that 'grain and drink offerings have been cut off from the house of the LORD,' Joel 1:9, the loss signals judgment. Malachi then promises that 'in every place, incense and pure offerings will be presented in My name,' Malachi 1:11, a vision of worship among the nations.

The New Testament takes up the chapter's ingredients. Leaven becomes an image for corruption that spreads, 'the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy,' Luke 12:1, and 'a little leaven works through the whole batch,' 1 Corinthians 5:6 and Galatians 5:9, though Jesus also uses it positively of the kingdom's growth, Matthew 13:33. Salt becomes a picture of disciples, Matthew 5:13, and of gracious speech, Colossians 4:6. Frankincense is laid before the child Jesus, Matthew 2:11. The angel tells Cornelius that his prayers and gifts 'have ascended as a memorial offering before God,' Acts 10:4, using the language of the memorial portion of verse 2 for a Gentile's prayer and charity.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to see that approach to God is not only about sin. The grain offering has no blood and no word of atonement. It is a gift, a tribute brought to the great King from the work of one's hands, and its place right after the burnt offering teaches that the God who accepts a substitute also receives His people's labour.

He wanted them to understand that such gifts are regulated by God's holiness. The flour must be fine, the frankincense given entire, and nothing leavened or sweetened may go up in smoke on the altar. God is not an idol to be fed with whatever the worshiper likes. The rules of verses 11 to 13 teach that even ordinary food, when brought to God, must be brought on His terms.

He wanted them to remember the covenant at every meal of worship. Salt was the one ingredient required 'to each of your offerings,' verse 13, and it is called 'the salt of the covenant of your God.' Every grain offering reminded the giver that this was not a transaction with a stranger but an act inside a binding relationship.

And he wanted Israel to support those who served at the altar. The repeated statement that the remainder belongs to Aaron and his sons made the people's gifts the priests' daily bread, and made the priests' food a holy thing.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The grain offering is prescribed law for Israel's sanctuary. Its specific rules, the handful burned, the remainder eaten by priests, no leaven on the altar, belonged to a system that Hebrews says was a shadow now fulfilled in Christ. Christians are not asked to burn flour or incense.

What the New Testament does carry forward is the pattern of offering. Believers are told to 'continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise,' Hebrews 13:15, and Paul calls gifts sent to support ministry 'a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice,' Philippians 4:18. The principle that those who serve at the altar live from its offerings is applied directly to gospel workers: 'those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel,' 1 Corinthians 9:13-14.

The prohibitions are also taken up, but as images, not rules. Paul's command to 'get rid of the old leaven' concerns malice and wickedness, not bread, 1 Corinthians 5:7-8. Leaven is not sinful in itself, since the firstfruits loaves of Leviticus 23:17 were baked with it and brought to God. Applying this chapter well means following the lines the New Testament itself draws, not turning every ingredient into a rule or a symbol.

debates.question: Why are leaven and honey kept off the altar, verse 11, while being acceptable as firstfruits, verse 12?

views.label: They represent corruption and decay
views.case: Leaven works by fermentation and honey ferments readily. An offering meant to rise to God as a pleasing aroma should not contain what spoils. This reading fits the Passover's removal of leaven, Exodus 12:15, and the New Testament's use of leaven for spreading sin, 1 Corinthians 5:6-8.

views.label: The line is about the altar, not the substance
views.case: Verse 12 explicitly permits both to be brought to the LORD as firstfruits, and Leviticus 23:17 prescribes two loaves 'baked with leaven, as the firstfruits.' Leaven also appears with the thanksgiving peace offering, Leviticus 7:13. So leaven and honey are not unclean in themselves; they are simply not burned on the altar.

views.label: A separation from other worship
views.case: Some suggest that honey and fermented offerings had a place in the worship of Israel's neighbours, so the ban marked Israel's altar as different. The text itself gives no reason, and this view depends on outside evidence rather than on anything Leviticus says.

debates.bearing: The text is clear on the rule and silent on the reason. The second view keeps us from overstating, since leaven can be offered in other ways. Yet the first view explains the pattern best, and the New Testament's own use of leaven builds on it. The altar receives only what does not spoil.

debates.question: What does 'the salt of the covenant' in verse 13 signify?

views.label: The permanence of the covenant
views.case: Salt preserves and does not itself decay. When Numbers 18:19 calls the priests' portion 'a permanent covenant of salt,' and 2 Chronicles 13:5 uses the phrase for God's covenant with David's house 'forever,' the stress falls on lasting validity. Salt in every offering declares that God's covenant does not spoil.

views.label: Covenant fellowship around a shared meal
views.case: Others note that covenants were often sealed with a meal, as at Sinai, Exodus 24:11, and that salt is the seasoning of every table. On this reading the grain offering is a covenant meal shared between God, who receives the memorial portion, and the priests, who eat the rest.

debates.bearing: Both ideas can stand together. The salt makes each offering part of a relationship that God binds Himself to keep. It reminded Israel that their worship took place inside a covenant God had made and would not abandon.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 opens with a surprising word. Chapter 1 began, 'When any of you brings,' using adam. Chapter 2 begins with nephesh, 'When anyone brings a grain offering,' the word often rendered 'soul' or 'life.' The change may simply be a variation of style, but it fits an offering the poorest could afford: whoever brings even flour brings as a whole person.

Minchah, the grain offering, is a word with a history. Its basic sense is a gift or tribute. Jacob sends a minchah to appease Esau, 'a gift for his brother,' Genesis 32:13. Ehud carries 'tribute to Eglon king of Moab,' Judges 3:15, and the conquered Moabites 'brought him tribute,' 2 Samuel 8:2. Cain's and Abel's offerings are both called minchah, Genesis 4:3-5. Leviticus narrows it to grain, but the older sense remains: this is what a subject brings to a king.

The 'memorial portion' of verses 2, 9 and 16 is azkarah, from the verb zakar, to remember. The word is used of the frankincense set by the Bread of the Presence, 'so that it may serve as a memorial portion,' Leviticus 24:7, and of the sin offering of flour in Leviticus 5:12. The idea is that the portion burned brings the worshiper before God to be remembered with favour. The Septuagint renders it with a Greek word for memorial, and Acts 10:4 uses that word of Cornelius' prayers and alms rising 'as a memorial offering before God.'

Levonah, frankincense, comes from the root for white, perhaps from the colour of the resin or its smoke. It is always given whole to God in this chapter; the priests eat the flour but never the incense.

The 'most holy' of verses 3 and 10 is qodesh qodashim, the superlative form that also names the inner sanctuary. The grain offering shares this highest grade of holiness with the sin and guilt offerings, Leviticus 6:17, and 'anything that touches them will become holy,' Leviticus 6:18.

Two words for leaven stand in verse 11. The first, chamets, is what has been leavened. The second, seor, is the leavening agent itself, the old dough kept back to start the next batch. Devash, honey, may include syrup from fruit as well as bees' honey, which suits the firstfruits of 2 Chronicles 31:5, where honey is listed among 'all the produce of the field.'

Verse 14 uses three farm words together: aviv, the fresh ears, the word that also names the month of Abib when Israel left Egypt, Exodus 13:4; 'roasted on the fire'; and geres karmel, crushed or coarsely ground new grain.

typology.fulfillment: The grain offering had to be free of what spoils and spreads. Peter says of Christ, 'He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth,' 1 Peter 2:22, and Paul, 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. Therefore let us keep the feast... with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth,' 1 Corinthians 5:7-8. The escalation is that Christ is not only free of corruption but is Himself 'the true bread from heaven,' John 6:32. The type falls short because flour is inert, while Jesus actively chose obedience at every point. Older typology that finds His humanity in the 'evenness' of fine flour goes beyond the text.

typology.type: The firstfruits offered to the LORD, verses 14 to 16
typology.fulfillment: The first ripe grain was brought to God before the harvest was eaten, a pledge that the rest belonged to Him too. Leviticus 23:10-11 has the sheaf of firstfruits waved 'on the day after the Sabbath.' Paul calls the risen Jesus 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, raised on the first day of the week. The escalation is that the firstfruits now guarantee a harvest of resurrection. The type falls short because roasted grain is consumed, while Christ's risen life is imperishable.

typology.type: The memorial portion rising to God
typology.fulfillment: A handful was burned so that the worshiper would be remembered before God, verse 2. Christ gave Himself 'as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God,' Ephesians 5:2, and on His account His people are remembered with favour. Cornelius' prayers are said to rise 'as a memorial offering,' Acts 10:4, and believers are to offer 'a sacrifice of praise,' Hebrews 13:15. The escalation is that the memorial is no longer a handful of flour but hearts and lips offered through Jesus. The type falls short because the handful had to be repeated; the offering that makes us welcome has been made once.

typology.type: The priest's portion, most holy food
typology.fulfillment: The remainder of the grain offering became the holy bread of the priests who had no land. Jesus pointed to the bread only priests could eat, Matthew 12:3-4, and then offered Himself as bread to His disciples, 'Take and eat; this is My body,' Matthew 26:26. Believers, now 'a royal priesthood,' 1 Peter 2:9, are fed by Him. The escalation is that a whole people of priests is nourished by the life of Christ Himself. The type falls short because the priests' bread merely sustained the body; Christ gives life to the world, John 6:33.

study.christ:
The grain offering is the chapter of bread, and Jesus calls Himself bread. 'It is My Father who gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is He who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world... I am the bread of life,' John 6:32-35. The manna is the direct background of that saying, but the grain offering helps fill it out. In Leviticus 2 a portion of fine bread goes up to God and the rest feeds His priests. In John 6 the bread comes down from God and feeds everyone who believes.

Jesus speaks of grain in another way that touches this chapter. 'Unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed; but if it dies, it bears much fruit,' John 12:24. The firstfruits of verse 14 were crushed and roasted over fire before they were offered. The New Testament does not tie John 12 to Leviticus 2 directly, so this is a resonance rather than a stated fulfilment, but Isaiah supplies the stronger line: 'He was crushed for our iniquities,' Isaiah 53:5.

The firstfruits lead to Christ more firmly. Leviticus 23:10-11 commands the sheaf of firstfruits to be waved before the LORD 'on the day after the Sabbath,' the first day of the week. Paul calls the risen Jesus 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20. The first sheaf promised a harvest; the risen Christ guarantees the resurrection of His people.

Paul also borrows the altar's language for the cross. Christ 'gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God,' Ephesians 5:2. The phrase 'pleasing aroma' is repeated for the grain offering in verses 2 and 9, and the cross is where that aroma rises fully. His whole life was a gift of tribute to the Father, and in that sense He fulfils the minchah as surely as the burnt offering.

Finally, the absence of leaven points to His purity. 'He committed no sin,' 1 Peter 2:22. Paul joins the two ideas directly: because 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' the church must be 'a new unleavened batch,' 1 Corinthians 5:7.

Two cautions help. First, the New Testament does not explain the oven, the griddle and the pan, and reading the three methods as three kinds of suffering is guesswork. Second, the grain offering is a gift, not an atonement, so its line to Christ runs through His offering of Himself to the Father and His feeding of His people, not through the shedding of blood. Read that way, the chapter shows the Son as the tribute Israel owed and the bread the priests needed.
study.god:
The grain offering shows a God who receives gifts. He does not need them, as Psalm 50:12 insists, but He welcomes them, and He sets out how they may be brought. A God who accepts flour and oil is a God who cares about the ordinary labour of His people, the ploughing, grinding and baking that filled their days. Nothing in their work was too small to be brought to Him.

He is the King to whom tribute is due. The word minchah was the tribute a subject paid a sovereign, Judges 3:15. Israel's God is not a household spirit to be fed but the great King whose people honour Him from their harvest. The frankincense, the costly part, goes wholly to Him.

He is holy, even in the kitchen. The remainder is 'most holy,' verse 3, and must be eaten in a holy place by the priests, Leviticus 6:16. God's holiness reaches into bread. There is no division here between the sacred and the everyday; the everyday is claimed for God and made holy by being given to Him.

He is a God who remembers. The memorial portion rises so that the worshiper will be remembered before Him, verse 2. God's remembering in Scripture is never mere recall; when 'God remembered Noah,' the waters began to subside, Genesis 8:1. The grain offering pictures a God who keeps His people in mind for good.

He is faithful in covenant. The salt required in every offering, verse 13, points to a covenant God has made and will not break, called elsewhere 'a permanent covenant of salt,' Numbers 18:19. Every time an Israelite seasoned an offering, he was reminded that his God is not changeable.

He provides for those who serve Him. The priests had no land because God Himself was their portion, Numbers 18:20. He fed them from the people's gifts, which shows His care for His servants and His purpose that worshipers and ministers depend on one another.

For worship the chapter invites us to bring our ordinary work to God as an offering, knowing that He receives it. It also asks us to bring it without the leaven of hypocrisy and with the salt of covenant faithfulness. And it assures us that we worship a God who remembers His people and keeps His promises.

crossReferences.note: Cain's fruit of the soil and Abel's firstborn of the flock are both called minchah, the word Leviticus 2 uses for the grain offering. The story shows from the start that God looks at the giver as well as the gift, a concern the prophets later press against empty offerings.

The priests' law of the grain offering. It fills in what Leviticus 2 assumes: the remainder must be eaten without leaven in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting, only by the males of Aaron's family, and it is most holy, so anything that touches it becomes holy.

Someone too poor to bring even two birds may bring fine flour as a sin offering, without oil or frankincense. It shows how far down the scale of cost God's provision reaches, and how a grain offering's memorial portion could be used for atonement in the case of poverty.

The sheaf of firstfruits is waved on the day after the Sabbath, and at the Feast of Weeks two loaves 'baked with leaven' are brought as firstfruits. This illuminates verse 12: leaven may be offered to God as firstfruits, only not burned on the altar.

The priests' portion of the holy offerings is called 'a permanent covenant of salt.' The phrase explains verse 13: the salt in each grain offering marks it as part of an unbreakable covenant, and ties the priests' food to God's lasting commitment to them.

David asks that his prayer rise like incense and his uplifted hands like 'the evening offering,' the minchah. The psalm shows the grain offering's meaning moving into prayer, preparing for the New Testament's language of spiritual sacrifices.

God promises that in every place, among the nations, 'incense and pure offerings' will be presented in His name. The word for offering is minchah, and the vision looks beyond Israel's one altar to worldwide worship, fulfilled as the gospel goes to the nations.

Jesus says the Father gives the true bread from heaven and that He is the bread of life. The grain offering fed the priests with holy bread; Jesus offers Himself as bread that gives life to the world to all who come to Him.

Paul warns that a little leaven works through the whole batch and calls the church to be a new unleavened batch because Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. The altar's refusal of leaven in verse 11 becomes a call to put away malice and wickedness.

Paul calls the risen Christ 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.' The firstfruits of verse 14, the first of the harvest given to God, become a picture of the resurrection of Jesus as the pledge of the harvest to come.

The angel tells Cornelius that his prayers and gifts to the poor have ascended 'as a memorial offering before God.' The memorial portion of Leviticus 2:2 becomes a way of describing a Gentile's prayers being remembered by God, the first step toward his hearing the gospel.

Paul calls the gifts the Philippians sent him 'a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well-pleasing to God.' As the grain offering fed the priests who served at the altar, the church's gifts sustain those who serve the gospel, and God receives them as worship.

study.oneStory:
At creation God gave the man and woman 'every seed-bearing plant' for food, Genesis 1:29, and the ground yielded freely. After the fall the ground was cursed and bread came 'by the sweat of your brow,' Genesis 3:19. The grain offering stands in that world of toil. It takes the product of cursed ground and hard labour and offers part of it back to God, confessing that the harvest is His gift and that the King is owed tribute.

The first offering outside Eden was a minchah, and it ended in murder, Genesis 4:3-8. From the start, what matters is not only the gift but the heart of the one who brings it. Leviticus 2 regulates the gift so that it comes on God's terms: fine flour, frankincense, no leaven, salt of the covenant. It also directs the gift to feed the priests, so that worship sustains those who serve.

The story then carries the grain offering through Israel's history. It rose every morning and evening with the burnt offering. Its loss in judgment was mourned by Joel. Its meaning moved into prayer in the Psalms, and Malachi foresaw pure offerings in every place among the nations.

In Christ the offering is fulfilled. He is the bread from heaven, the one who gave Himself as a fragrant offering, the grain that fell into the earth and died and bore much fruit, and the firstfruits raised on the first day of the week. Through Him the church offers the sacrifice of praise and gifts that sustain the gospel's servants.

The story ends at a table. The curse on the ground will be lifted, Revelation 22:3, and the tree of life will yield 'a fresh crop for each month,' Revelation 22:2. Those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9, will eat in God's presence without toil and without end, and all their labour will have been received by the King to whom it was always owed.

quiz.q: What three ingredients make up the basic grain offering?

options.text: Fine flour, olive oil, and frankincense.
options.note: Verse 1 lists these three elements as the core of the grain offering.
Honey is explicitly forbidden in the fire offering, verse 11; this is not the correct combination.
Salt is required, but yeast, leaven, is explicitly forbidden, and water is not named as an ingredient.
Verse 1 gives a specific and detailed list of ingredients.

quiz.q: What happens to the remainder of the grain offering after the memorial portion is burned?

options.text: It belongs to Aaron and his sons as a most holy portion.
options.note: Verses 3 and 10 both state this explicitly.

options.text: It is thrown away as unclean.
options.note: The remainder is not discarded; it is a most holy portion given to the priests.

options.text: It is returned to the worshiper to eat at home.
options.note: The remainder belongs to the priests, not back to the one who brought the offering.

options.text: The whole offering is always burned completely, with nothing left over.
options.note: Only a memorial handful is burned; the remainder belongs to the priests.

quiz.q: What two things must never be included in a grain offering burned on the altar?

options.note: Verse 11 explicitly forbids both leaven and honey in offerings made by fire.
These are required ingredients of the grain offering, not forbidden ones.

quiz.q: How is the firstfruits grain offering, verses 14 to 16, to be prepared?

options.text: As crushed heads of new grain, roasted on the fire, with oil and frankincense added.
options.note: Verses 14 to 15 describe exactly this preparation.

options.note: Oil and frankincense are explicitly added, verse 15.

questions: The grain offering brought the ordinary produce of daily labor to God. What part of your everyday work or income have you never thought to offer to Him?
Leaven and honey, associated with corruption and decay, were kept out of the offering. What corrupting influence do you need to remove before you can worship God with an undivided heart?
Salt, the sign of the covenant, was never to be left out. Where do you need reminding that God's covenant faithfulness to you does not decay or run out?
Most of the grain offering fed the priests who served at the altar. How well do you support those who give their lives to serving God's people?
Christ is the bread of life, offered without the leaven of sin. What would it look like this week to feed on Him rather than on the corrupting things you are tempted to consume instead?

translationNotes.note: Grain offering translates minchah, a word that elsewhere in the Old Testament describes a tribute or gift brought to a king or superior, framing this bloodless offering as homage to God as Israel's true Sovereign.
Leaven, se'or, and honey, devash, were likely excluded from the altar because both ferment or spoil readily, unsuited to an offering meant to picture purity and permanence before God.
The salt of the covenant of your God echoes ancient Near Eastern treaty language, where salt symbolized a binding, enduring agreement, compare Numbers 18:19 and 2 Chronicles 13:5.
